:knowledge-point/canonical-example.:question/problem: What is the equation of the tangent to the curve $x = 2y^2 -y + 1$ at the point $(2,1)?$
:knowledge-point/canonical-example.:question/worked-solution:
First, we differentiate $x(y)$ with respect to $y{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}y} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}y}(2{y}^{2}-y+1) \\  & =2\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}y}({y}^{2})-\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}y}(y)+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}y}(1) \\  & =2\cdot (2y)-1+0 \\  & =4y-1\end{aligned}
$$

Now, taking the reciprocal of $\dfrac{\textrm dx}{\textrm dy},$ we get

$$
\dfrac{\textrm dy}{\textrm dx} = \left( \dfrac{\textrm dx}{\textrm dy} \right)^{-1} = \dfrac1{4y - 1}.
$$

The slope of the tangent to the curve at the point $(2,1)$ is 

$$
\begin{aligned}m & =\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}{|}_{(x,y)=(2,1)} \\  & =\frac{1}{4(1)-1} \\  & =\frac{1}{3}.\end{aligned}
$$

Using the point-slope formula for a tangent line, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}y-{y}_{1} & =m(x-{x}_{1}) \\ y-1 & =\frac{1}{3}(x-2) \\ y & =\frac{x}{3}-\frac{2}{3}+1 \\ y & =\frac{x}{3}+\frac{1}{3}.\end{aligned}
$$

:knowledge-point/questions.:question/problem: Given a curve $x=\frac{2}{3}{y}^{3}-{y}^{2},$ what is the equation of the tangent to the curve at the point $(9,3)?$
:knowledge-point/questions.:question/worked-solution:
First, we differentiate $x(y)$ with respect to $y:$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}y} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}y}(\frac{2}{3}{y}^{3}-{y}^{2}) \\  & =\frac{2}{3}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}y}({y}^{3})-\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}y}({y}^{2}) \\  & =\frac{2}{3}\cdot 3{y}^{2}-2y \\  & =2{y}^{2}-2y\end{aligned}
$$

Now, taking the reciprocal of $\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}y},$ we get

$$
\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}={\left(\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}y}\right)}^{-1}=\frac{1}{2{y}^{2}-2y}.
$$

The slope of the tangent to the curve at the point $(9,3)$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}m & =\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}{|}_{(x,y)=(9,3)} \\  & =\frac{1}{2(3)^{2}-2(3)} \\  & =\frac{1}{12}.\end{aligned}
$$

Using the point-slope formula for a tangent line, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}y-{y}_{1} & =m(x-{x}_{1}) \\ y-3 & =\frac{1}{12}(x-9) \\ y & =\frac{x}{12}-\frac{3}{4}+3 \\ y & =\frac{x}{12}+\frac{9}{4}.\end{aligned}
$$

:knowledge-point/questions.:question/problem: Given a curve $x = \sqrt{y} - \frac{1}{2y}$, what is the equation of the tangent to the curve at the point $(\frac{1}{2}, 1)$?
Given a curve $x=6{y}^{2}+2y-5,$ what is the equation of the tangent to the curve at the point $(3,1)?$
:knowledge-point/questions.:question/worked-solution:
First, we differentiate $x(y)$ with respect to $y:$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}y} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}y}(6{y}^{2}+2y-5) \\  & =6\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}y}({y}^{2})+2\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}y}(y)-5\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}y}(1) \\  & =6\cdot (2y)+2(1)+0 \\  & =12y+2.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, taking the reciprocal of $\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}y},$ we get

$$
\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}={\left(\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}y}\right)}^{-1}=\frac{1}{12y+2}.
$$

The slope of the tangent to the curve at the point $(3,1)$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}m & =\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}{|}_{(x,y)=(3,1)} \\  & =\frac{1}{12\cdot 1+2} \\  & =\frac{1}{14}.\end{aligned}
$$

Using the point-slope formula for a tangent line, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}y-{y}_{1} & =m(x-{x}_{1}) \\ y-1 & =\frac{1}{14}(x-3) \\ y & =\frac{x}{14}-\frac{3}{14}+1 \\ y & =\frac{x}{14}+\frac{11}{14}.\end{aligned}
$$

First, we differentiate $x(y)$ with respect to $y:$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}y} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}y}({y}^{2}-2y\sqrt{y}) \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}y}({y}^{2})-2\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}y}(y\sqrt{y}) \\  & =2y-2\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}y}(y\cdot {y}^{1/2})-0 \\  & =2y-2\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}y}({y}^{3/2}) \\  & =2y-2\cdot \frac{3}{2}{y}^{1/2} \\  & =2y-3{y}^{1/2} \\  & =2y-3\sqrt{y}\end{aligned}
$$

Now, taking the reciprocal of $\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}y},$ we get

$$
\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}={\left(\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}y}\right)}^{-1}=\frac{1}{2y-3\sqrt{y}}.
$$

The slope of the tangent to the curve at the point $(0,4)$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}m & =\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}{|}_{(x,y)=(0,4)} \\  & =\frac{1}{2(4)-3\sqrt{4}} \\  & =\frac{1}{8-6} \\  & =\frac{1}{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Using the point-slope formula for a tangent line, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}y-{y}_{1} & =m(x-{x}_{1}) \\ y-4 & =\frac{1}{2}(x-0) \\ y & =\frac{1}{2}x+4.\end{aligned}
$$

:knowledge-point/questions.:question/problem: Given a curve $x=5{y}^{3}-8{y}^{2}+16,$ what is the equation of the tangent to the curve at the point $(24,2)?$
:knowledge-point/questions.:question/worked-solution:
First, we differentiate $x(y)$ with respect to $y:$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}y} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}y}(5{y}^{3}-8{y}^{2}+16) \\  & =5\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}y}({y}^{3})-8\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}y}({y}^{2})+16\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}y}(1) \\  & =5\cdot (3{y}^{2})-8\cdot (2y)+0 \\  & =15{y}^{2}-16y.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, taking the reciprocal of $\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}y},$ we get

$$
\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}={\left(\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}y}\right)}^{-1}=\frac{1}{15{y}^{2}-16y}.
$$

The slope of the tangent to the curve at the point $(24,2)$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}m & =\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}{|}_{(x,y)=(24,2)} \\  & =\frac{1}{15\cdot {2}^{2}-16\cdot 2} \\  & =\frac{1}{28}.\end{aligned}
$$

Using the point-slope formula for a tangent line, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}y-{y}_{1} & =m(x-{x}_{1}) \\ y-2 & =\frac{1}{28}(x-24) \\ y & =\frac{x}{28}-\frac{6}{7}+2 \\ y & =\frac{x}{28}+\frac{8}{7}.\end{aligned}
$$

:knowledge-point/questions.:question/problem: Given a curve $x=5{y}^{5}-3{y}^{3},$ what is the equation of the tangent to the curve at the point $(-2,-1)?$
:knowledge-point/questions.:question/worked-solution:
First, we differentiate $x(y)$ with respect to $y:$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}y} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}y}(5{y}^{5}-3{y}^{3}) \\  & =5\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}y}({y}^{5})-3\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}y}({y}^{3}) \\  & =5\cdot (5{y}^{4})-3\cdot (3{y}^{2}) \\  & =25{y}^{4}-9{y}^{2}\end{aligned}
$$

Now, taking the reciprocal of $\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}y},$ we get

$$
\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}={\left(\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}y}\right)}^{-1}=\frac{1}{25{y}^{4}-9{y}^{2}}.
$$

The slope of the tangent to the curve at the point $(-2,-1)$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}m & =\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}{|}_{(x,y)=(-2,-1)} \\  & =\frac{1}{25(-1)^{4}-9(-1)^{2}} \\  & =\frac{1}{16}.\end{aligned}
$$

Using the point-slope formula for a tangent line, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}y-{y}_{1} & =m(x-{x}_{1}) \\ y-(-1) & =\frac{1}{16}(x-(-2)) \\ y+1 & =\frac{1}{16}(x+2) \\ y & =\frac{x}{16}+\frac{2}{16}-1 \\ y & =\frac{x}{16}+\frac{1}{8}-1 \\ y & =\frac{x}{16}-\frac{7}{8}.\end{aligned}
$$

:knowledge-point/questions.:question/problem: Given a curve $x=y+\frac{3}{{y}^{3}},$ what is the equation of the tangent to the curve at the point $(4,1)?$
:knowledge-point/questions.:question/worked-solution:
First, we differentiate $x(y)$ with respect to $y:$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}y} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}y}(y+\frac{3}{{y}^{3}}) \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}y}(y)+3\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}y}\left(\frac{1}{{y}^{3}}\right) \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}y}(y)+3\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}y}({y}^{-3}) \\  & =1+3\cdot (-3{y}^{-4}) \\  & =1-9{y}^{-4} \\  & =1-\frac{9}{{y}^{4}} \\  & =\frac{{y}^{4}-9}{{y}^{4}}.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, taking the reciprocal of $\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}y},$ we get

$$
\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}={\left(\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}y}\right)}^{-1}=\frac{{y}^{4}}{{y}^{4}-9}.
$$

The slope of the tangent to the curve at the point $(4,1)$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}m & =\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}{|}_{(x,y)=(4,1)} \\  & =\frac{{1}^{4}}{{1}^{4}-9} \\  & =-\frac{1}{8}.\end{aligned}
$$

Using the point-slope formula for a tangent line, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}y-{y}_{1} & =m(x-{x}_{1}) \\ y-1 & =-\frac{1}{8}(x-4) \\ y & =-\frac{x}{8}+\frac{1}{2}+1 \\ y & =-\frac{x}{8}+\frac{3}{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

:knowledge-point/questions.:question/problem: Given a curve $x=\frac{1}{\sqrt{y}}-2{y}^{2},$ what is the equation of the tangent to the curve at the point $(-1,1)?$
:knowledge-point/questions.:question/worked-solution:
First, we differentiate $x(y)$ with respect to $y:$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}y} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}y}(\frac{1}{\sqrt{y}}-2{y}^{2}) \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}y}\left(\frac{1}{\sqrt{y}}\right)-2\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}y}({y}^{2}) \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}y}({y}^{-1/2})-2\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}y}({y}^{2}) \\  & =-\frac{1}{2}{y}^{-3/2}-2\cdot (2y) \\  & =-\frac{1}{2{y}^{3/2}}-4y \\  & =\frac{-1-8{y}^{5/2}}{2{y}^{3/2}} \\  & =-\frac{1+8{y}^{2}\sqrt{y}}{2y\sqrt{y}}.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, taking the reciprocal of $\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}y},$ we get

$$
\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}={\left(\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}y}\right)}^{-1}=-\frac{2y\sqrt{y}}{1+8{y}^{2}\sqrt{y}}.
$$

The slope of the tangent to the curve at the point $(-1,1)$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}m & =\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}{|}_{(x,y)=(-1,1)} \\  & =-\frac{2(1)\sqrt{1}}{1+8(1)^{2}\sqrt{1}} \\  & =-\frac{2}{9}.\end{aligned}
$$

Using the point-slope formula for a tangent line, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}y-{y}_{1} & =m(x-{x}_{1}) \\ y-1 & =-\frac{2}{9}(x-(-1)) \\ y & =-\frac{2}{9}x-\frac{2}{9}+1 \\ y & =-\frac{2}{9}x+\frac{7}{9}.\end{aligned}
$$

:knowledge-point/questions.:question/problem: Given a curve $x=\sqrt{{y}^{3}}+\frac{1}{{y}^{2}},$ what is the equation of the tangent to the curve at the point $(2,1)?$
:knowledge-point/questions.:question/worked-solution:
First, we differentiate $x(y)$ with respect to $y:$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}y} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}y}(\sqrt{{y}^{3}}+\frac{1}{{y}^{2}}) \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}y}(\sqrt{{y}^{3}})+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}y}\left(\frac{1}{{y}^{2}}\right) \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}y}({y}^{3/2})+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}y}({y}^{-2}) \\  & =\frac{3}{2}{y}^{1/2}-2{y}^{-3} \\  & =\frac{3{y}^{1/2}}{2}-\frac{2}{{y}^{3}} \\  & =\frac{3{y}^{7/2}-4}{2{y}^{3}}.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, taking the reciprocal of $\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}y},$ we get

$$
\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}={\left(\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}y}\right)}^{-1}=\frac{2{y}^{3}}{3{y}^{7/2}-4}.
$$

The slope of the tangent to the curve at the point $(2,1)$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}m & =\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}{|}_{(x,y)=(2,1)} \\  & =\frac{2(1)^{3}}{3(1)^{7/2}-4} \\  & =-2.\end{aligned}
$$

Using the point-slope formula for a tangent line, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}y-{y}_{1} & =m(x-{x}_{1}) \\ y-1 & =-2(x-2) \\ y & =-2x+4+1 \\ y & =-2x+5.\end{aligned}
$$

:knowledge-point/questions.:question/problem: Given a curve $x=4{y}^{2}+\frac{1}{{y}^{2}}-1,$ what is the equation of the tangent to the curve at the point $(4,1)?$

First, we differentiate $x(y)$ with respect to $y:$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}y} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}y}(4{y}^{2}+\frac{1}{{y}^{2}}-1) \\  & =4\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}y}({y}^{2})+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}y}\left(\frac{1}{{y}^{2}}\right)-\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}y}(1) \\  & =4\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}y}({y}^{2})+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}y}({y}^{-2})-\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}y}(1) \\  & =4\cdot (2y)-2{y}^{-3}-0 \\  & =8y-\frac{2}{{y}^{3}} \\  & =\frac{8{y}^{4}-2}{{y}^{3}}.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, taking the reciprocal of $\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}y},$ we get

$$
\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}={\left(\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}y}\right)}^{-1}=\frac{{y}^{3}}{8{y}^{4}-2}.
$$

The slope of the tangent to the curve at the point $(4,1)$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}m & =\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}{|}_{(x,y)=(4,1)} \\  & =\frac{(1)^{3}}{8(1)^{4}-2} \\  & =\frac{1}{6}.\end{aligned}
$$

Using the point-slope formula for a tangent line, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}y-{y}_{1} & =m(x-{x}_{1}) \\ y-1 & =\frac{1}{6}(x-4) \\ y & =\frac{x}{6}-\frac{2}{3}+1 \\ y & =\frac{x}{6}+\frac{1}{3}.\end{aligned}
$$
